Interface dynamics of the porous medium equation with a bistable reaction term

Abstract

We consider a degenerate partial differential equation arising in population dynamics, namely the porous medium equation with a bistable reaction term. We study its asymptotic behavior as a small parameter, related to the thickness of a diffuse interface, tends to zero. We prove the rapid formation of transition layers which then propagate. We prove the convergence to a sharp interface limit whose normal velocity, at each point, is that of the underlying degenerate travelling wave.

Key Words: degenerate diffusion, singular perturbation, sharp interface limit, population dynamics.22 2 AMS Subject Classifications: 35K65, 35B25, 35R35, 92D25.

1 Introduction

In this paper we consider the rescaled porous medium equation with a bistable reaction term

(Pε){ut=ε​Δ​(um)+1ε​f​(u)in ​Ω×(0,∞)∂(um)∂ν=0on ​∂Ω×(0,∞)u​(x,0)=u0​(x)in ​Ω,(P^{\;\!\varepsilon})\quad\begin{cases}u_{t}=\varepsilon\Delta(u^{m})+\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}f(u)&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial(u^{m})}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)&\text{in }\Omega\,,\end{cases}

and study the sharp interface limit as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. Here Ω\Omega is a smooth bounded domain in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} (N≥2N\geq 2), ν\nu is the Euclidian unit normal vector exterior to ∂Ω\partial\Omega and m>1m>1.

We assume that ff is smooth, has exactly three zeros 0<a<10<a<1 such that

f′​(0)<0,f′​(a)>0,f′​(1)<0,f^{\prime}(0)<0\,,\qquad f^{\prime}(a)>0\,,\qquad f^{\prime}(1)<0\,, (1.1)

and that

∫01m​um−1​f​(u)​𝑑u>0.\int_{0}^{1}mu^{m-1}f(u)\,du>0\,. (1.2)

The above assumption implies that the speed of the underlying degenerate travelling wave is positive (see subsection 3.1), so that the region enclosed by the limit interface is expanding (see below). This explains why the requirement (1.2) is convenient for the study of invasion processes.

As far as the initial data is concerned, we assume that 0≤u0≤M0\leq u_{0}\leq M (for some M>aM>a) is a C2​(Ω¯)C^{2}(\overline{\Omega}) function with compact support

S​u​p​p​u0:=Cl⁡{x∈Ω:u0​(x)>0}⊂⊂Ω.Supp\,u_{0}:={\rm Cl}\{x\in\Omega:\,u_{0}(x)>0\}\subset\subset\Omega\,.

Furthermore we define the initial interface Γ0\Gamma_{0} by

Γ0:={x∈Ω:u0​(x)=a},\Gamma_{0}:=\{x\in\Omega:\,u_{0}(x)=a\}\,,

and suppose that Γ0\Gamma_{0} is a smooth hypersurface without boundary, such that, nn being the Euclidian unit normal vector exterior to Γ0\Gamma_{0},

Γ0⊂⊂Ω and ∇u0(x)≠0if x∈Γ0 ,\Gamma_{0}\subset\subset\Omega\quad\mbox{ and }\quad\nabla u_{0}(x)\neq 0\quad\text{if $x\in\Gamma_{0}$\,,} (1.3)
u0>a in Ω0(1),u0<a in Ω0(0),u_{0}>a\quad\text{ in }\quad\Omega_{0}^{(1)}\,,\quad u_{0}<a\quad\text{ in }\quad\Omega_{0}^{(0)}\,, (1.4)

where Ω0(1)\Omega_{0}^{(1)} denotes the region enclosed by Γ0\Gamma_{0} and Ω0(0)\Omega_{0}^{(0)} the region enclosed between ∂Ω\partial\Omega and Γ0\Gamma_{0}.

Problem (Pε)(P^{\;\!\varepsilon}) possesses a unique weak solution uεu^{\varepsilon} as it is explained in Section 2. As ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, by formally neglecting the diffusion term, we see that, in the very early stage, the value of uεu^{\varepsilon} quickly becomes close to either 11 or 00 in most part of Ω\Omega, creating a steep interface (transition layers) between the regions {uε≈1}\{u^{\varepsilon}\approx 1\} and {uε≈0}\{u^{\varepsilon}\approx 0\}. Once such an interface develops, the diffusion term is large near the interface and comes to balance with the reaction term. As a result, the interface ceases rapid development and starts to propagate in a slower time scale. Therefore the limit solution u~​(x,t)\tilde{u}(x,t) will be a step function taking the value 11 on one side of the moving interface, and 00 on the other side.

We shall prove that this sharp interface limit, which we denote by Γt\Gamma_{t}, obeys the law of motion

(P 0){Vn=c∗ on ​ΓtΓt|t=0=Γ0,(P^{\;\!0})\quad\begin{cases}\,V_{n}=c^{*}\quad\text{ on }\Gamma_{t}\vskip 3.0pt\\ \,\Gamma_{t}\big|_{t=0}=\Gamma_{0}\,,\end{cases}

where VnV_{n} is the normal velocity of Γt\Gamma_{t} in the exterior direction, and c∗c^{*} the positive speed of the underlying travelling wave (see subsection 3.1). Problem (P 0)(P^{\;\!0}) possesses a unique smooth solution on [0,Tm​a​x)[0,T^{max}) for some Tm​a​x>0T^{max}>0. We denote this solution by Γ=∪0≤t<Tm​a​x(Γt×{t})\Gamma=\cup_{0\leq t<T^{max}}(\Gamma_{t}\times\{t\}). From now on, we fix 0<T<Tm​a​x0<T<T^{max} and work on [0,T][0,T].

We set

QT:=Ω×(0,T),Q_{T}:=\Omega\times(0,T)\,,

and, for each t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], we denote by Ωt(1)\Omega_{t}^{(1)} the region enclosed by the hypersurface Γt\Gamma_{t}, and by Ωt(0)\Omega_{t}^{(0)} the region enclosed between ∂Ω\partial\Omega and Γt\Gamma_{t}. We define a step function u~​(x,t)\tilde{u}(x,t) by

u~​(x,t):={ 1in ​Ωt(1) 0in ​Ωt(0)for ​t∈[0,T],\tilde{u}(x,t):=\begin{cases}\,1&\text{in }\Omega_{t}^{(1)}\\ \,0&\text{in }\Omega_{t}^{(0)}\end{cases}\quad\text{for }t\in[0,T]\,, (1.5)

which represents the formal asymptotic limit of uεu^{\varepsilon} as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Our main result, Theorem 1.1, describes both the emergence and the propagation of the layers. First, it gives the profile of the solution after a very short initial period: the solution uεu^{\varepsilon} quickly becomes close to 11 or 00, except in a small neighborhood of the initial interface Γ0\Gamma_{0}, creating a steep transition layer around Γ0\Gamma_{0} (generation of interface). The time needed to develop such a transition layer, which we will denote by tεt^{\varepsilon}, is 𝒪⁡(ε​|ln⁡ε|)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|). Then the theorem states that the solution uεu^{\varepsilon} remains close to the step function u~\tilde{u} on the time interval [tε,T][t^{\varepsilon},T] (motion of interface).

Theorem 1.1 (Generation and motion of interface).

Assume m≥2m\geq 2. Define μ\mu as the derivative of f⁡(u)f(u) at the unstable equilibrium u=au=a, that is

μ=f′​(a).\mu=f^{\prime}(a)\,.

Let η∈(0,min⁡(a,1−a))\eta\in(0,\min(a,1-a)) be arbitrary. Fix α0>0\alpha_{0}>0 arbitrarily small. Then there exist positive constants ε0\varepsilon_{0} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that, for all ε∈(0,ε0)\,\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}) and for all (x,t)(x,t) such that tε≤t≤T\,t^{\varepsilon}\leq t\leq T, where

tε:=μ−1​ε​|ln⁡ε|,t^{\varepsilon}:=\mu^{-1}\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|\,, (1.6)

we have

uε​(x,t)∈{[1−2​ε,1+η]ifx∈Ωt(1)∖𝒩𝒞​ε​|ln⁡ε|​(Γt)[0,1+η]ifx∈Ω[0,η]ifx∈Ωt(0)∖𝒩α0​(Γt),u^{\varepsilon}(x,t)\in\begin{cases}\,[1-2\varepsilon,1+\eta]&\quad\text{if}\quad x\in\Omega_{t}^{(1)}\setminus\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{C}\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|}(\Gamma_{t})\\ \,[0,1+\eta]&\quad\text{if}\quad x\in\Omega\\ \,[0,\eta]&\quad\text{if}\quad x\in\Omega_{t}^{(0)}\setminus\mathcal{N}_{\alpha_{0}}(\Gamma_{t})\,,\end{cases} (1.7)

where 𝒩r​(Γt):={x∈Ω:d​i​s​t​(x,Γt)<r}\mathcal{N}_{r}(\Gamma_{t}):=\{x\in\Omega:\,dist(x,\Gamma_{t})<r\} denotes the rr-tubular neighborhood of Γt\Gamma_{t}.

Remark 1.2 (About the thickness of the interface).

Since the construction of super-solutions is much more involved than that of sub-solutions, the statement (1.7) is more accurate in Ωt(1)\Omega_{t}^{(1)} than in Ωt(0)\Omega_{t}^{(0)}. More precisely, on the one hand, (1.7) shows that the convergence to 1 is uniform “inside the interface” except in 𝒪⁡(ε​|ln⁡ε|)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|) tubular neighborhoods of the sharp interface limit; on the other hand, (1.7) only shows that the convergence to 0 is uniform “outside the interface” except in 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) tubular neighborhoods of the sharp interface limit.

Remark 1.3 (About the assumption m≥2m\geq 2).

Note that the sub- and super-solutions we shall construct to study the motion of interface allow m>1m>1. Nevertheless, since we consider not well-prepared initial data, we need to quote a generation of interface result from [2] which is valid only for m≥2m\geq 2 (if 1<m<21<m<2 the partial differential equation is not only degenerate but also singular). When initial data have a “suitable shape”, the restriction m≥2m\geq 2 can be removed.

As a direct consequence of Theorem 1.1, we have the following convergence result.

Corollary 1.4 (Convergence).

Assume m≥2m\geq 2. As ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, the solution uεu^{\varepsilon} converges to u~\tilde{u} in ∪0<t≤T(Ωt(i)×{t})\cup_{0<t\leq T}(\Omega^{(i)}_{t}\times\{t\}), where i=0,1i=0,1.

For the relevance of nonlinear diffusion in population dynamics models, we refer the reader to Gurney and Nisbet [9], Gurtin and Mac Camy [10]: density dependent diffusion is efficient to study the dynamics of a population which regulates its size below the carrying capacity set by the supply of nutrients. Since density dependent equations degenerate at points where u=0u=0, a loss of regularity of solutions occurs and their support propagates at finite speed.

Let us mention some earlier works on problems involving nonlinear diffusion that are related to ours. Feireisl [6] has studied the singular limit of (Pε)(P^{\;\!\varepsilon}) in the whole space ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}, which allows to reduce the issue to the radially symmetric case. Hilhorst, Kersner, Logak and Mimura [11] have investigated the singular limit of the equation posed in a bounded domain of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}, with f⁡(u)f(u) of the Fisher-KPP type. Note that the authors in [11] assume the convexity of Ω0(1)\Omega_{0}^{(1)} which allows them to construct a single super-solution for both the generation and the motion of interface. Here, we dot not make such a geometric assumption.

The organization of this work is as follows. In Section 2, we briefly recall known results concerning the well-posedness of Problem (Pε)(P^{\;\!\varepsilon}). Section 3 is the body of the paper: we construct sub- and super-solutions to study the motion of the transition layers. Finally, we prove Theorem 1.1 in Section 4.

2 Comparison principle, well-posedness

Since the diffusion term degenerates when u=0u=0 a loss of regularity of solutions occurs. We define below a notion of weak solution for Problem (Pε)(P^{\;\!\varepsilon}), which is very similar to the one proposed by Aronson, Crandall and Peletier [3] for the one dimensional problem with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Concerning the initial data, we suppose here that u0∈L∞​(Ω)u_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega) and u0≥0u_{0}\geq 0 a.e. Note that in this subsection, and only in this subsection, we assume, without loss of generality, that ε=1\varepsilon=1, which yields the Problem

(P){ut=Δ⁡(um)+f⁡(u)in ​Ω×(0,∞)∂(um)∂ν=0on ​∂Ω×(0,∞)u​(x,0)=u0​(x)in ​Ω.(P)\quad\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta(u^{m})+f(u)&\text{in }\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial(u^{m})}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{on }\partial\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)&\text{in }\Omega\,.\end{cases}
Definition 2.1.

A function u:[0,∞)→L1​(Ω)u:[0,\infty)\to L^{1}(\Omega) is a solution of Problem (P)(P) if, for all T>0T>0,

  1. (i)

    u∈C⁡([0,∞),L1​(Ω))∩L∞​(QT);u\in C\left([0,\infty);L^{1}(\Omega)\right)\cap L^{\infty}(Q_{T})\,;

  2. (ii)

    for all φ∈C2​(QT¯)\varphi\in C^{2}(\overline{Q_{T}}) such that φ≥0\varphi\geq 0 and ∂φ∂ν=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\nu}=0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega, it holds that

    ∫Ωu⁡(T)​φ​(T)−∫∫QT(u​φt+um​Δ​φ)=∫Ωu0​φ​(0)+∫∫QTf⁡(u)​φ.\int_{\Omega}u(T)\varphi(T)-\int\int_{Q_{T}}(u\varphi_{t}+u^{m}\Delta\varphi)=\int_{\Omega}u_{0}\varphi(0)+\int\int_{Q_{T}}f(u)\varphi\,. (2.1)

A sub-solution (respectively a super-solution) of Problem (P)(P) is a function satisfying (i) and (ii) with equality replaced by ≤\leq (respectively ≥\geq).

Theorem 2.2 (Existence and comparison principle).

The following properties hold.

  1. (i)

    Let u−u^{-} and u+u^{+} be a sub-solution and a super-solution of Problem (Pε)(P^{\varepsilon}) with initial data u0−u_{0}^{-} and u0+u_{0}^{+} respectively.

    If u0−≤u0+a.e. then u−≤u+​ in ​QT;\mbox{If~}\quad u_{0}^{-}\leq u_{0}^{+}\,\quad{a.e.}\quad\mbox{~then~}\quad u^{-}\leq u^{+}\mbox{~in~}Q_{T}\,;
  2. (ii)

    Problem (P)(P) has a unique solution uu on [0,∞)[0,\infty) and

    0≤u≤max⁡(1,‖u0‖L∞​(Ω)) in ​QT;0\leq u\leq\max(1,\|u_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})\quad\mbox{~in~}Q_{T}\,; (2.2)
  3. (iii)

    u∈C⁡(QT¯)u\in C(\overline{Q_{T}}).

The proof of the theorem above can be performed in the same lines as in [3, Theorem 5] (see also [13] and [4] for related results). The continuity of uεu^{\varepsilon} follows from [5].

The following result turns out to be an essential tool when constructing smooth sub- and super-solutions of Problem (Pε)(P^{\;\!\varepsilon}).

Lemma 2.3.

Let uu be a continuous nonnegative function in Ω¯×[0,T]\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]. Define Ωt⋆={x∈Ω:u⁡(x,t)>0}\Omega_{t}^{\star}=\{x\in\Omega:\,u(x,t)>0\} and Γt⋆=∂Ωt⋆\Gamma_{t}^{\star}=\partial\Omega_{t}^{\star} for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Suppose the family Γ:=∪0<t≤TΓt⋆×{t}\Gamma:=\cup_{0<t\leq T}\Gamma_{t}^{\star}\times\{t\} is sufficiently smooth and let νt⋆\nu_{t}^{\star} be the outward normal vector on Γt⋆\Gamma_{t}^{\star}. Suppose moreover that

  1. (i)

    ∇(um) is continuous in Ω¯×[0,T]\nabla(u^{m})\text{ is continuous in }\ \overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]

  2. (ii)

    ℒ⁡[u]:=ut−Δ⁡(um)−f⁡(u)=0​ in ​{(x,t)∈Ω¯×[0,T]:u⁡(x,t)>0}{\cal L}[u]:=u_{t}-\Delta(u^{m})-f(u)=0\;\text{ in }\ \{(x,t)\in\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T]:\,u(x,t)>0\}

  3. (iii)

    ∂(um)∂νt⋆=0​ on ​∂Ωt⋆, for all ​t∈[0,T]\displaystyle{\frac{\partial(u^{m})}{\partial\nu_{t}^{\star}}}=0\;\text{ on }\ \partial\Omega_{t}^{\star},\;\text{ for all }\ t\in[0,T] .

Then uu is a solution of Problem (P)(P). Similarly a sub-solution (respectively a super-solution) of Problem (P)(P) is a function satisfying (i) and (ii)—(iii) with equality replaced by ≤\leq (respectively ≥\geq).

The proof of this result can be found in [11].

3 Motion of the transition layers

3.1 Materials

Underlying travelling waves. Hosono [12] has investigated travelling wave solutions for the degenerate one dimensional equation

ut=(um)x​x+f⁡(u).u_{t}=(u^{m})_{xx}+f(u)\,.

He proved that there exists a unique travelling wave (c∗,U)(c^{*},U), that the sign of the velocity c∗c^{*} is that of ∫01um−1​f​(u)​𝑑u\int_{0}^{1}u^{m-1}f(u)\,du, and that the profiles vary with the sign of the velocity. More precisely, for c∗<0c^{*}<0, the front is smooth and U∈C∞​(ℝ)U\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), whereas, for c∗>0c^{*}>0, we only have (Um−1)′∈L∞​(ℝ)({U}^{m-1})^{\prime}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), but (Um−1)′∉C⁡(ℝ)({U}^{m-1})^{\prime}\notin C(\mathbb{R}). These different behaviors of the travelling waves are in contrast with the density independent diffusion models, where fronts are smooth whatever their velocities are (see [7]).

In the present paper, the assumption (1.2) implies that c∗>0c^{*}>0. More precisely the following holds (see [12] for details). The travelling wave (c∗,U)(c^{*},U) is the solution of the auxiliary problem

{(Um)′′+c∗​U′+f⁡(U)=0 on ​(−∞,ω)U⁡(−∞)=1U⁡(0)=aU′<0 on ​(−∞,ω)(Um)′​(ω)=0U≡0 on [ω,∞),\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}({U}^{m})^{\prime\prime}+c^{*}U^{\prime}+f(U)=0&\text{ on }(-\infty,\omega)\\ U(-\infty)=1\\ U(0)=a\\ {U}^{\prime}<0&\text{ on }(-\infty,\omega)\\ ({U}^{m})^{\prime}(\omega)=0\\ U\equiv 0&\text{ on }[\omega,\infty)\,,\end{array}\right. (3.1)

for some ω>0\omega>0. As z→−∞z\to-\infty, terms are exponentially decaying:

max⁡(1−U⁡(z),|U′​(z)|,|U′′​(z)|)≤C​e−λ​|z| for ​z≤0,\max\left(1-U(z),|{U}^{\prime}(z)|,|{U}^{\prime\prime}(z)|\right)\leq Ce^{-\lambda|z|}\quad\text{ for }z\leq 0\,, (3.2)

for some positive constants CC and λ\lambda. As z↗ωz\nearrow\omega, we have

limz↗ω(Um−1)′​(z)=−m−1m​c∗ and limz↗ω(Um−1)′′​(z)=−(m−1)2m2​f′​(0),\lim_{z\nearrow\omega}\left({U}^{m-1}\right)^{\prime}(z)=-\frac{m-1}{m}c^{*}\quad\text{ and }\quad\lim_{z\nearrow\omega}({U}^{m-1})^{\prime\prime}(z)=-\frac{(m-1)^{2}}{m^{2}}f^{\prime}(0)\,, (3.3)

and U′(ω)∈[−∞,0)U^{\prime}(\omega)\in[-\infty,0). Moreover, for a positive constant which we denote again by CC, there holds

|(Um)′′​(z)|≤C​|U′​(z)|=−C​U′​(z) for all ​z∈(−∞,ω).|(U^{m})^{\prime\prime}(z)|\leq C|U^{\prime}(z)|=-CU^{\prime}(z)\quad\text{ for all }z\in(-\infty,\omega)\,. (3.4)

The cut-off signed distance function. Another classical ingredient in similar situations (see [14] or [8]) is a cut-off signed distance function dd which we now define. Let d~​(⋅,t)\widetilde{d}(\cdot,t) be the signed distance function to Γt\Gamma_{t}, namely

d~​(x,t):={−dist⁡(x,Γt) for ​x∈Ωt(1)dist⁡(x,Γt) for ​x∈Ωt(0),\widetilde{d}(x,t):=\begin{cases}-&\hskip-10.0pt{\rm dist}(x,\Gamma_{t})\quad\text{ for }x\in\Omega_{t}^{(1)}\\ &\hskip-10.0pt{\rm dist}(x,\Gamma_{t})\quad\text{ for }x\in\Omega_{t}^{(0)}\,,\end{cases} (3.5)

3.2 Construction of sub-solutions

Equipped with the travelling wave (c∗,U)(c^{*},U) and the signed distance function dd, we are looking for sub-solutions in the form

uε−​(x,t):=(1−ε)​U​(d⁡(x,t)+ε​|ln⁡ε|​p​etε)=(1−ε)​U​(zε−​(x,t)),u^{-}_{\varepsilon}(x,t):=(1-\varepsilon)U\left(\frac{d(x,t)+\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|p\,e^{t}}{\varepsilon}\right)=(1-\varepsilon)U(z^{-}_{\varepsilon}(x,t))\,, (3.11)

where

zε−​(x,t):=d⁡(x,t)+ε​|ln⁡ε|​p​etε.z^{-}_{\varepsilon}(x,t):=\displaystyle\frac{d(x,t)+\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|p\,e^{t}}{\varepsilon}\,. (3.12)
Lemma 3.1 (Sub-solutions).

Let p>0p>0 be arbitrary. Then, for ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough, uε−u^{-}_{\varepsilon} is a sub-solution for Problem (Pε)(P^{\;\!\varepsilon}).

Proof.

In this proof (and only in this proof) we set uε−=uu^{-}_{\varepsilon}=u and zε−=zz^{-}_{\varepsilon}=z. Note that

Ωt⋆={x∈Ω:d⁡(x,t)<−ε​|ln⁡ε|​p​et+ε​ω},\Omega_{t}^{\star}=\{x\in\Omega:\,d(x,t)<-\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|p\,e^{t}+\varepsilon\omega\}\,, (3.13)

where Ωt⋆\Omega_{t}^{\star} is defined as in Lemma 2.3. It follows that u≡0u\equiv 0 near the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega so that the Neumann boundary condition (i​i​i)(iii) in Lemma 2.3 is fulfilled. 3.3 Construction of super-solutions

The construction of super-solutions is more involved: since we want them to be positive it is no longer possible to use the natural travelling wave (c∗,U)(c^{*},U) which is compactly supported. Therefore we shall first consider slightly larger speeds c>c∗c>c^{*} which provide faster travelling wave solutions which tend to +∞+\infty in −∞-\infty; then a small modification will provide us positive and more regular functions which are “nearly” travelling wave solutions. Before making this argument more precise, let us note that, as it will clearly appear below, the possibility of the above strategy follows from [12].

Let η∈(0,min⁡(a,1−a))\eta\in(0,\min(a,1-a)) be arbitrary. Let α0>0\alpha_{0}>0 be fixed. 4 Proof of Theorem 1.1

4.1 A generation of interface property

We first state a result on the generation of interface.

Lemma 4.1 (Generation of interface).

Assume m≥2m\geq 2. Let η>0\eta>0 be arbitrary small. Then, for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega, we have, for ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough,

and there exists M0>0M_{0}>0 such that, for ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough,

u0​(x)≤a−M0​ε​|ln⁡ε|⟹uε​(x,tε)≤ε,\displaystyle u_{0}(x)\leq a-M_{0}\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|\Longrightarrow u^{\varepsilon}(x,t^{\varepsilon})\leq\varepsilon\,, (4.3)

We only give an outline since the arguments can be found in [1], [2].

[Y⁡(tεε,u0​(x)−ε2​C∗​(eμ​tε/ε−1))]+≤uε​(x,tε)≤[Y⁡(tεε,u0​(x)+ε2​C∗​(eμ​tε/ε−1))]+.\left[Y\left(\frac{t^{\varepsilon}}{\varepsilon};\,u_{0}(x)-\varepsilon^{2}C^{*}(e^{\mu t^{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon}-1)\right)\right]^{+}\\ \leq u^{\varepsilon}(x,t^{\varepsilon})\leq\left[Y\left(\frac{t^{\varepsilon}}{\varepsilon};\,u_{0}(x)+\varepsilon^{2}C^{*}(e^{\mu t^{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon}-1)\right)\right]^{+}\,.

Next a straightforward modification of [1, Lemma 3.9] —which specifies the instability of the equilibrium Y≡aY\equiv a and the stability of the equilibria Y≡0Y\equiv 0, Y≡1Y\equiv 1— shows that for ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough, for all ξ∈(−1,2)\xi\in(-1,2), we have

and that

ξ≤a−ε​|ln⁡ε|⟹Y⁡(μ−1​|ln⁡ε|,ξ)≤ε.\displaystyle\xi\leq a-\varepsilon|\ln\varepsilon|\Longrightarrow Y(\mu^{-1}|\ln\varepsilon|;\xi)\leq\varepsilon\,.

The combination of the above arguments completes the proof of the lemma. ∎

4.2 Proof of the main theorem

We are now in the position to prove Theorem 1.1. To that purpose we show that solutions are in between the propagation of interface sub- and super-solutions at time tεt^{\varepsilon}.

Proof.

Assume m≥2m\geq 2. Let η∈(0,min⁡(a,1−a))\eta\in(0,\min(a,1-a)) be arbitrary. First note that the comparison principle directly implies that inequality (4.1) persists for later times, i.e.
